questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
Bologna is the ultimate student city. With the University of Bologna, the city is packed with young people from all over the world. It has this lively, welcoming vibe where it’s super easy to meet new people, whether it's at a café, a piazza, or during one of the many student events. You’ll never feel alone here, everyone is in the same boat, looking for new experiences and friendships.

Food is a major part of any exchange experience. And in Bologna, it’s next-level. This city is the heart of Italian cuisine, known for tagliatelle al ragù, tortellini, and mortadella. Eating out is affordable for students, and there are tons of cozy osterias where you can get authentic, home style Italian food without breaking the bank.

One of the best things about Bologna is its size. It’s big enough to have everything you need, bars, clubs, concerts, markets, parks, but small enough that you don’t feel lost in a massive city. You can walk or bike everywhere, which makes life super convenient. Plus, the city is full of stunning medieval architecture, and you’ll find yourself strolling under its endless porticoes no matter the weather.

Bologna is right in the middle of Italy, which means you can easily take a train and be in Florence, Venice, Milan, or even Rome in just a few hours. The airport also has cheap flights all over Europe, making weekend trips super easy.

If you want a city full of students, great food, a buzzing nightlife, and a deep history, Bologna should be at the top of your list. It’s the perfect balance between study and fun, tradition and modern life. By the time your exchange is over, you won’t want to leave.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
Finding the necessary information upon arrival in Bologna wasn't the easiest, as a lot of it had to be actively searched for rather than being readily available. There wasn’t a single clear guide for everything, so I had to ask around, check university websites, and rely on other students' experiences to figure things out.

That being said, the information is there, you just have to look for it. While response times from some offices could be slow, especially for administrative matters, most things could be sorted out with some patience and persistence. Connecting with other exchange students and asking in Facebook groups or WhatsApp chats was often the fastest way to get answers.

Overall, it requires some effort, but you’ll find what you need if you take the initiative.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer:
When I arrived in Bologna, there was an online help desk available for new students, which was really useful. However, because so many students were logging in at the start of the semester, there were some delays in the process. It’s important to be patient, as it might take a few days to get fully checked in, even after starting your courses.

That said, once you’re through the initial wait, the staff are very friendly and helpful, and the system works well. They made sure all my questions were answered and helped with any issues I had. It just requires a bit of patience at the beginning.

Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
The registration process at the University of Bologna is mainly done online, and getting through it can be challenging due to high demand at the beginning of the semester. The check-in system requires patience, as it can take several days before everything is finalized, even after classes have started.

There isn’t really a physical office where you can go for direct help. If you try, you’ll likely be sent from one faculty to another without getting clear answers. However, once you do get through the online process, the staff are helpful and responsive, making sure everything is sorted out properly.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Online help desk

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer:
Registering for classes at the University of Bologna was very easy. The system allowed me to add and drop courses without much hassle, which was great in case a class didn’t turn out as expected. This flexibility made it simple to adjust my schedule and find the courses that best suited my interests.

The university staff were helpful and understanding when it came to switching courses, so overall, the process was smooth and student friendly.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be patient. The registration process can take time, especially with the online check-in system. It might take a few days before everything is finalized, so don’t stress if things aren’t immediately sorted. Stay persistent, check for updates regularly, and reach out for help if needed. Once you get through it, everything runs smoothly

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
The difficulty level of courses at the University of Bologna was quite varied. Some courses were relatively easy, while others were more challenging, depending on the subject and professor. The structure and expectations were different from what I was used to in Denmark, making the experience both interesting and sometimes unpredictable.

There was also a big difference in exam formats. Unlike in Denmark, where exams tend to follow a more standardized structure, exams in Bologna could be multiple-choice, oral exams, handwritten written exams, or take-home assignments. This variety required adaptability, but it also provided a unique learning experience.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
The teaching style at the University of Bologna was quite similar to that at UCPH in terms of academic approach. However, one key difference was the class size here, the groups were much smaller, creating a more classroom-like atmosphere.

Professors were very interactive, frequently asking questions and expecting students to engage actively in discussions. This made the lessons more dynamic but also meant that participation was expected, rather than just listening passively.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Visualizing The Italian Society – The professor is truly passionate about Italian culture and does a great job of bringing it to life through film analysis. The course is engaging and offers a unique perspective on how Italian society is represented in cinema.

Education Systems and Policies – This course is great for understanding higher education systems across different countries, especially since many exchange students share insights from their home universities. It provides a broad, comparative perspective that makes discussions both interesting and relevant.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
One of the biggest unexpected costs was rent, especially if you want to live within the city walls. Housing prices can be quite high compared to other Italian cities.

Another thing to be aware of is that imported groceries (anything not from Italy) are often more expensive than in Denmark. If you prefer certain international brands or ingredients, you might end up paying more than expected.

Finally, there are a lot of small expenses that add up things like social activities, transportation, and everyday essentials. It’s just part of the exchange experience, but it’s good to budget for these extra costs.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Rent can be quite high, especially within the city walls. Imported groceries, such as non-Italian brands or specific international products, are also noticeably more expensive than in Denmark. Eating out frequently can add up, even though many student friendly options exist. Everyday essentials and small purchases, like coffee or transport, can also accumulate into a larger expense than anticipated.

Local Italian groceries, especially fresh produce, pasta, and cheese, are very affordable compared to Denmark. Eating at traditional osterias or student canteens can be relatively cheap if you choose wisely. Public transport is also reasonably priced, though Bologna is very walkable, reducing the need for it.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
The University Sports Centre (CUSB) provides numerous opportunities for students to engage in various sports at subsidized rates. Available activities include football, swimming, tennis, and more. CUSB also organizes tournaments and university championships, fostering a vibrant athletic community. 

Students can immerse themselves in a rich cultural scene through exhibitions, concerts, lectures, and other events organized by the university. The Collegium Musicum offers students the chance to join choirs or the orchestra, providing a platform to share their passion for music in a dynamic and international environment. 

Numerous student associations are active within the university, covering a broad spectrum of interests and providing ample opportunities for social engagement. These associations organize events, workshops, and gatherings, enhancing the social experience on campus. 

Additionally, the university offers incentives for students to spend their free time at theaters, cinemas, or participating in various leisure activities, further enriching the student experience.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Bologna is perfectly located for traveling. You can easily take a train to Florence, Venice, Milan, or Rome for a weekend. It is a great way to explore more of Italy while on exchange

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
In Bologna
Climb the Asinelli Tower – Get the best panoramic view of the city from the top of this medieval tower.
Explore the Quadrilatero Market – A historic market area full of great food, local delicacies, and a true Italian atmosphere.
Visit San Luca Sanctuary – Walk the world's longest portico (covered walkway) up to this beautiful hilltop basilica.
Enjoy Bologna’s Nightlife – Areas like Via del Pratello and Piazza Verdi are full of student-friendly bars and a great atmosphere.
Discover the Hidden Canals – Bologna has a secret system of canals; check out the "Finestrella di Via Piella" for a unique view.
Easy Weekend Trips from Bologna
Florence (40 min by train) – Home to incredible art, museums, and beautiful streets. A must-see.
Venice (1.5 hours by train) – The canals, gondolas, and historic charm make it a perfect weekend getaway.
Milan (1 hour by train) – Visit the Duomo, go shopping, and experience the fashion capital of Italy.
Verona (1.5 hours by train) – See Juliet’s balcony and the beautiful historic city center.
Rimini (1 hour by train) – If you want a beach day, this is the best place to relax by the Adriatic Sea.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer:
Adjusting to the local culture in Bologna was quite easy, especially because it is such a student-friendly city. The atmosphere is welcoming, and since there are so many international students, you never feel out of place.

One of the biggest cultural differences is the Italian pace of life. Things move a bit slower, especially with bureaucracy, so patience is key. Meals are also a big social event, with dinner often starting late in the evening.

The locals are friendly and open, but it helps to know a few basic Italian phrases, as not everyone speaks English fluently. Learning simple greetings and ordering food in Italian makes a big difference in daily interactions.

Overall, the combination of a vibrant student community, great food, and a relaxed lifestyle made it easy to settle in and feel at home in Bologna.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
The best way to connect with local students is simple. Just talk to them. Italians are incredibly friendly and love to chat, so do not be afraid to start a conversation. Even if some of them are not completely confident in English, they are usually eager to talk and will often help you learn some Italian along the way.

Many students enjoy discussing food, culture, and everyday life, so even small talk can lead to new friendships. Whether it is during class, at a café, or in a bar, just be open, ask questions, and show interest. You will quickly find that most Italians are happy to engage and include you in their social circles.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
One of the biggest challenges was adjusting to the slow pace of bureaucracy. Things like university registration, administrative processes, and even simple tasks such as getting official documents processed could take much longer than expected. Patience is essential when dealing with these situations.

Another noticeable difference was the daily schedule. Italians eat much later than in Denmark, with dinner often starting around 8 or 9 in the evening. At first, it took some time to adjust, but eventually, it became a fun part of the experience.

The concept of time is also more relaxed. Being slightly late is normal, and schedules are often more flexible. While this creates a laid-back atmosphere, it can sometimes be frustrating when you are used to a more punctual culture.

Finally, although many Italians are very friendly and talkative, not everyone speaks fluent English. This could make communication difficult at times, especially in smaller shops or with older locals. However, learning a few basic Italian phrases helped a lot in these situations.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer:
One of the things I appreciated most was how social and welcoming Italians are. People love to talk, whether it is in class, at a café, or even in the supermarket. It makes the city feel warm and inviting, especially for exchange students.

I also really enjoyed the food culture. Meals are not just about eating but about spending time together. Whether it is a long dinner with friends or a casual aperitivo, food is an important part of daily life, and it creates a great sense of community.

Another thing I loved was the relaxed lifestyle. While it takes time to get used to the flexible concept of time, it also creates a more enjoyable and less stressful environment. People take their time to enjoy life rather than rushing through it.

Finally, Bologna’s history and architecture added so much to the experience. Walking through the beautiful old streets, surrounded by porticoes and historic buildings, made everyday life feel special. The city has a unique charm that is hard to find anywhere else.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Be patient with bureaucracy
Things like university registration and administrative processes take time. The online check-in can be slow, and response times can be long. Do not stress if things are not sorted right away. Just stay persistent, check for updates regularly, and ask other students for help if needed.

Enjoy the food culture
Bologna is known as the food capital of Italy, and eating here is more than just a necessity. It is a social and cultural experience. Try traditional dishes like tagliatelle al ragù, tortellini, and mortadella. Go to local osterias, enjoy aperitivo in the evening, and embrace the slower, more relaxed way of dining.

Take advantage of Bologna’s location
Bologna is one of the best cities in Italy for travel. With fast train connections to Florence, Venice, Milan, and Rome, you can easily explore Italy during weekends and holidays. The airport also has cheap flights to other European destinations, so make sure to plan some trips while you are there.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Do not get a bike. It will most likely be stolen, and the only affordable options are in poor condition.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer:
The most rewarding part of my exchange experience was living in Bologna, a city that is truly special in every way. The atmosphere is incredible, filled with friendly and passionate people who make you feel welcome from day one. Whether it is chatting with locals at a café, meeting students from all over the world, or simply walking through the historic streets, Bologna has a unique energy that makes everyday life exciting.

The food culture was another highlight. Bologna is the heart of Italian cuisine, and every meal feels like an experience. From the best tagliatelle al ragù to late-night aperitivos with friends, food is a central part of life here, and you can truly taste the love and tradition in every dish.

The city’s dedication to football also adds to its charm. Whether you are watching Bologna FC play at the stadium or just experiencing the passion for football in bars and cafés, the love for the sport is everywhere. The locals live and breathe football, and it brings people together in a way that is amazing to witness.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer:
One of the biggest challenges during my exchange was navigating the Italian way of doing things, especially when it came to bureaucracy and university administration. From the very start, the online check-in process tested my patience, with long waiting times and slow responses. Getting simple things like course registrations or official documents sorted out often felt like an endless cycle of being sent from one office to another.

Another challenge was adapting to the unpredictability of daily life. In Denmark, things run on schedule, and information is usually clear. In Bologna, plans can change last minute, whether it is a professor moving an exam date or a shop randomly closing in the middle of the day for pausa pranzo. At first, this was frustrating, but over time, I learned to embrace the more relaxed Italian mindset and go with the flow.

Language was also an obstacle at times. While many young Italians speak English, a lot of day-to-day interactions, buying groceries, dealing with landlords, or asking for directions—happened in Italian. Not knowing the language fluently made some situations tricky, but the locals were always friendly and eager to help, even if it meant a mix of broken Italian, hand gestures, and Google Translate.

Despite these challenges, every difficulty came with a lesson. I learned to be patient, adapt quickly, and not stress over small things. Looking back, overcoming these obstacles made my exchange even more rewarding and helped me grow both personally and academically.
